subject: Operating Systems
title: Discover FCFS Scheduling
description: Discover how the CPU runs ready processes in their arrival order.

mission.title: Run the Ready Queue
mission.description: Follow each process from the ready queue to the CPU and then to completion.

quiz.question: In FCFS scheduling, which process runs first?

discovery.title: Arrival Order Decides
discovery.summary: FCFS scheduling runs processes in the same order they arrive in the ready queue.

sections.title: What is a process?
sections.content: A process is a program that is currently ready to run or is running on the computer.

sections.title: What is CPU scheduling?
sections.content: CPU scheduling decides which ready process gets to use the CPU next.

sections.title: Ready queue
sections.content: The ready queue holds processes that are waiting for CPU time.

sections.title: What is FCFS?
sections.content: FCFS means First Come, First Served.

sections.title: Arrival order
sections.content: Processes run in the same order that they arrive in the ready queue.

sections.title: Advantage
sections.content: FCFS is simple to understand and easy to implement.

sections.title: Disadvantage
sections.content: A long process at the front can make short processes wait for a long time.

sections.title: Convoy effect
sections.content: The convoy effect happens when many short processes are stuck waiting behind one long process, like cars behind a slow truck.

alternate_explanations.title: Think of a checkout line
alternate_explanations.content: FCFS works like a checkout line. The person who arrives first is served first, even if someone behind them has only one item.

alternate_explanations.title: Follow the ready queue
alternate_explanations.content: The ready queue starts P1(4), P2(2), P3(3). P1 uses the CPU and finishes first, then P2 runs, then P3. Their arrival order never changes.

introduction.title: Meet FCFS Scheduling
introduction.content: A computer has one CPU, so it needs a rule for choosing which waiting program runs next. FCFS uses arrival order.
points: Ready processes wait in a queue.
The process at the front gets the CPU first.
You will follow processes from waiting to running to completed.

worked_example.title: Follow the first arrival
worked_example.content: P1 arrived before P2 and P3, so FCFS gives P1 the CPU first.

steps.explanation: P1 is first in line because it arrived first.
P1 moves from the front of Ready Queue into the CPU.
P1 finishes before P2 gets a turn; FCFS does not skip ahead.

worked_example.conclusion: First Come, First Served keeps the same arrival order from start to finish.

next.title: Run the ready queue.
next.content: Use NEXT STEP to watch every process move through the CPU.

action_explanations.observe-ready-queue: P1 is at the front, so its earlier arrival gives it the first CPU turn.
action_explanations.run-first-process: P1 keeps the CPU while it executes; FCFS does not interrupt it for a later arrival.
action_explanations.finish-p1: P1 is complete, so the next process waiting at the front can run.
action_explanations.run-next-process: P2 now runs because it has waited at the front since P1 left.
action_explanations.complete-all: P3 finishes last because it arrived after P1 and P2.

challenge.continue_message: Challenge complete. Keep exploring to see how a long process can delay the ones behind it.

phases.title: Serve the first arrival
phases.instruction: Move P1 through the CPU before allowing another process to run.

target.label: Goal
target.description: P1 should be completed first because it was first in the ready queue.

phases.feedback: Look at the front of the ready queue: FCFS always begins there.

phases.title: Keep the arrival order
phases.instruction: Finish the remaining processes in their waiting order.

target.label: Goal
target.description: P2 must complete before P3; neither process may jump ahead.

phases.feedback: Keep moving the front process through the CPU, then take the next process from the front.

recall.title: Recall
recall.prompt: In your own words, why does FCFS run P1 before P2 in this lesson?
recall.empty_message: Write a short explanation before submitting.
recall.model_answer: FCFS chooses the process that arrived first. P1 is at the front of the ready queue, so it gets the CPU before P2 and P3.

guidance.start_message: Choose which process should enter the CPU next.

items.content: FCFS always selects the process at the front of Ready Queue.

phases.title: Run the first arrival
phases.instruction: Complete P1 first, then continue in arrival order.
phases.feedback: Look at the front of Ready Queue.

guidance.start_message: Different burst times do not change FCFS arrival order.

items.content: Burst time changes how long a process runs, not who starts first.

phases.title: Keep arrival order
phases.instruction: Complete every process in FCFS order with less guidance.

target.label: TARGET
target.description: Arrival order remains P1 → P2 → P3.

phases.feedback: The first arrival never gets skipped in FCFS.

guidance.start_message: Derive the full execution order with no hints.

phases.title: Solve the schedule
phases.instruction: Complete the full schedule in strict arrival order.

target.label: TARGET
target.description: No shorter process may jump ahead.

phases.feedback: FCFS means first come, not shortest burst.

phases.instruction: Complete the randomized Ready Queue without hints.

target.label: TARGET
target.description: Every process must run exactly in arrival order.

phases.feedback: Use arrival order, not burst size, to decide.
